title: Shipment Pricing Refactor
flaw: Same carrier-type conditional chain duplicated across three functions (Strategy-shaped gap); primitive obsession on a raw carrier string instead of a literal union; boolean-parameter trap on isExpress/isFragile; magic-number rate literals scattered per branch.

title: Patient Vitals Monitor
flaw: An interval-driven polling effect subscribes to a vitals stream but never clears the interval on unmount or when the patientId prop changes, so switching patients stacks up concurrent pollers that keep writing stale readings into state for the wrong patient.
key_learnings: Correctly identified that intervals were piling up when patientId changed, confirmed via a console.log counter showing multiple concurrent polls.
mistakes: Added a patientId check inside the interval callback to ignore stale updates instead of clearing the interval itself - this stops the symptom (wrong readings) but leaves the leaked intervals running forever, still polling the network/API for no reason.
Did not add a cleanup function returned from useEffect.
Final test run: 3/5 passing - the two tests asserting the interval count after patient switches and after unmount still fail.
next_focus: Review what useEffect's cleanup function is for and when React calls it (every re-run of the effect, and on unmount) - this is the actual fix, not filtering inside the callback.
Practice spotting 'effect starts something ongoing' (interval/subscription/listener) as an immediate reflex to check for a matching teardown.

title: Watchlist Quote Panel
flaw: A debounced search-as-you-type ticker lookup fires an async quote fetch per keystroke with no request-sequencing guard, so a slower earlier response can resolve after a faster later one and overwrite the panel with stale quote data for a ticker the user already changed away from.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed the race: identified that fetch responses were being applied in resolution order rather than request order, and that the debounce alone doesn't prevent an in-flight stale request from still resolving late.

Implemented a request-id guard (incrementing a ref/counter per fetch, only applying the response if its id matches the latest issued request) rather than trying to cancel the fetch itself - a reasonable, idiomatic fix for this shape of race.
Verified the fix against the test that simulates out-of-order resolution (fast ticker B resolving before slow ticker A) and confirmed the panel now shows B's quote, not A's stale one.
mistakes: Initially reached for clearing a timeout-based debounce id as the fix, conflating 'debounce the trigger' with 'guard the response' - these are separate concerns and fixing only the debounce timing would not have addressed already-in-flight requests.
review_changes: Walked through why debouncing the call and sequencing the response are two different problems: debounce reduces how many requests go out, but does nothing once multiple are already in flight.
Ran the full suite after the fix: 4/4 passing, including the out-of-order resolution case.
next_focus: When multiple async calls can be in flight from rapid user input, default to asking 'what stops a stale response from overwriting a fresher one' as a separate question from 'how do I reduce the number of calls' - debounce/throttle and response-sequencing solve different halves of the problem.

title: Username Availability Field
flaw: Same stale-closure-async-race family as exercise 3 but in a different shape: an availability-check effect reads a ref-cached 'last submitted value' for comparison, but the ref is updated synchronously before the async check resolves, so by the time the async check's .then() runs, the ref no longer reflects the value that check was actually for - causing it to incorrectly treat its own now-stale response as still current.

title: Ranked Queue Service
flaw: MatchmakingQueue exposes its internal players array directly via a getter, and the UI component sorts/splices that same array reference in place to reorder the display - so reordering the display list silently reorders the actual matchmaking queue's internal priority, with no copy boundary between 'what the queue owns' and 'what the UI is allowed to touch'. NOTE: originally generated as a debugging exercise by mistake (incorrectly held category per old pre-fix progression logic, picked a bug-mechanism pattern for an architecture-tradeoffs slot) - regenerated correctly here as architecture-tradeoffs/broken-encapsulation under the corrected spec.
key_learnings: Correctly identified the shared-reference hazard: the UI's sortedForDisplay() was mutating the exact array instance returned by queue.players, not a copy, so Array.prototype.sort/splice calls meant to be 'just for display' were silently reordering the real matchmaking queue.

Fixed it by having the queue expose a defensive copy (players getter returns [...this._players]) rather than asking every call site to remember to copy - closes the leak at the source instead of relying on caller discipline.

Verified understanding by articulating why a defensive-copy getter is preferable to a 'please don't mutate this' comment: comments don't stop a future caller, a copy structurally can't be mutated into the original.
review_changes: Ran the test that sorts the returned players array and then checks the queue's internal match order is unchanged: passes against the fix.

Discussed the bonus extension (a readonly-array return type) as a complementary, compile-time-only layer on top of the runtime copy - agreed the copy is still required since a type annotation alone doesn't stop a .sort() call at runtime, only flags it if TypeScript's checked.
next_focus: When a class/module hands back a reference to its own internal mutable collection (array, Map, Set, or object), default-check: can the caller mutate this and have it silently affect the owner's internal state? If yes, that's broken encapsulation even with no crash or type error anywhere.

title: Payroll Event Processor
flaw: A PayrollEvent type uses optional fields (hourlyRate?, salaryAmount?, bonusAmount?, bonusReason?) to represent three mutually-exclusive event kinds (hourly, salaried, bonus) instead of a discriminated union, so nothing stops an object claiming kind: 'bonus' from also carrying a salaryAmount, and the processing function's if/else chain checking which fields happen to be present (rather than switching on a tag) silently mis-processes a malformed event instead of being caught at compile time - illegal states are representable, and there's no exhaustiveness check if a new kind is added.
key_learnings: Correctly modeled the three event kinds as a discriminated union on a kind: 'hourly' | 'salaried' | 'bonus' tag, with each variant only carrying the fields that actually apply to it (hourlyRate+hoursWorked for hourly, salaryAmount for salaried, bonusAmount+bonusReason for bonus) - eliminating the illegal 'bonus event with a salaryAmount' states the original optional-field shape allowed.

Replaced the field-presence if/else chain in processPayrollEvent with a switch (event.kind), and added a default case that assigns event to a never-typed variable - correctly explained this as an exhaustiveness check that will fail to compile if a fourth kind is ever added without updating this function.

Verified the union actually prevents the original bug: tried constructing a bonus-kind object with a stray salaryAmount field and confirmed TypeScript now rejects it at the construction site, where before it would have type-checked fine and been silently mis-processed.
mistakes: First draft kept hourlyRate and hoursWorked as two separate optional fields on the hourly variant rather than both required together, so an hourly event with hoursWorked but no hourlyRate (or vice versa) still type-checked - a smaller-scale recurrence of the same illegal-state gap one level down. Caught this unprompted on a second pass before review by re-reading the variant and asking whether any of ITS fields were secretly co-required, and made both required on that variant.
review_changes: Ran the test suite against the refactor: all passing, including the new test that confirms the malformed bonus+salaryAmount object fails to compile (checked via a dedicated type-level assertion rather than a runtime test).

Asked what would happen if a fifth event kind were added without touching processPayrollEvent - correctly traced through that the exhaustiveness check's default branch would now fail to compile because event would no longer be narrowed to never, catching the omission immediately rather than silently falling through at runtime.
next_focus: This exercise's own self-correction is the lesson worth keeping explicit: after modeling one discriminated union, re-check each individual variant for the same smell one level down - are any of THIS variant's own fields secretly mutually exclusive or co-required with each other, not just across variants.

title: Product Grid Search
flaw: ProductGrid passes a fresh inline onAddToCart={(id) => handleAdd(id)} closure and a fresh inline sortOptions={{key: 'relevance'}} object to a React.memo-wrapped ProductCard on every parent render (including on every keystroke in the unrelated search box), defeating the memo and re-rendering every card in the grid on each keystroke instead of only the cards whose visible data actually changed.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed that React.memo's shallow prop comparison was failing not because ProductCard's own data changed, but because the parent was handing it new function/object identities every render regardless of whether their contents differed.

Fixed onAddToCart by wrapping it in useCallback with the correct dependency array, and fixed sortOptions by hoisting the literal out of the render body (module-level constant, since it never actually varies) rather than wrapping it in useMemo for a value that was static all along - correctly reasoned that useMemo would have been unnecessary overhead for something that never changes.

Verified the fix using the test's render-count spy per card: confirmed typing in the search box no longer increments render counts for cards whose props didn't change, while a genuine data change (e.g. a price update) still re-renders only the affected card.
review_changes: Walked through why useCallback alone wasn't enough for sortOptions - useCallback memoizes functions, not plain objects - and confirmed the distinction was already understood rather than needing correction.

Discussed the bonus question (what happens if handleAdd's own identity changes every render) and correctly traced that useCallback's dependency array would need handleAdd listed if it weren't itself stable, otherwise the memoized onAddToCart would silently go stale.
next_focus: Keep distinguishing 'this value is expensive to recompute' (useMemo's actual job) from 'this value just needs a stable identity' (useCallback, or - as in the sortOptions case here - sometimes just hoisting a constant out of the component entirely, since not everything stable needs a hook at all).

title: Lineup Eligibility Rules
flaw: canAddToLineup and canCompleteTrade independently re-implement the same player-eligibility rule rather than sharing one source of truth, and the two copies have already drifted: canAddToLineup blocks injured_reserve players from any slot except ir_slot, but canCompleteTrade never grew that check (its comment says IR players historically couldn't be traded at all), so a trade can currently place an injured_reserve player directly into a starter slot - a duplicated-business-rule-gone-stale smell rather than a crash. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. Second appearance of code-review (exercise 1 was first, diff 1, still unreviewed), held at difficulty 2.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed and fixed the actual drift: extracted a single shared `handleSlotRestriction(player, slot)` helper and routed both `canAddToLineup` and `canCompleteTrade` through it, so the suspended/injured_reserve checks live in exactly one place and the two surfaces can no longer disagree about the same player/slot combination - matches the exercise's explicit goal.

Passing `destinationSlot` straight through to the shared helper rather than ignoring it meant the extraction didn't reintroduce an unused-parameter situation, even with the exercise's tsconfig already relaxed for that case.
mistakes: Left the pre-existing test 'currently allows trading an injured_reserve player straight into a starter slot' (which asserts `toBe(true)`) completely unchanged, even though the fix's entire purpose is to make that `false` now. Running the suite against the submitted fix shows 7/8 passing with exactly that one failure - a real regression against the test file as it stands, not a flaw in the production logic.
Declined to update that test when flagged, so the exercise is being logged with correct production code sitting behind a red test suite.
review_changes: Verified the fix with `tsc --noEmit` (clean) and the full test suite (7/8 passing), confirming the single failure is the pre-existing bug-documenting test rather than a new regression introduced by the refactor.

Explained why that specific test needs to change despite the README's 'maintain the spirit of the original test' restriction: that test's entire spirit was 'this is the current, not-yet-fixed bug,' and the fix's job is specifically to invalidate it - keeping its assertion frozen just pins the regression back in.
next_focus: Go back and flip that one test to `expect(...).toBe(false)` (and rename it away from 'currently allows...') so the suite is actually green - the only remaining step to close this exercise out cleanly.

When a fix is explicitly meant to change observable behavior rather than just internal structure, check for any test that documents the OLD behavior as current/expected - 'maintain the spirit of the original test' doesn't apply when a test's whole spirit was 'this is the bug to be fixed.'

title: Now Playing Crossfade
flaw: A crossfade effect schedules a setTimeout to swap tracks and starts a new audio fade, keyed on trackId, but the effect's cleanup only clears the timeout - not the in-flight Web Audio gain-ramp it already started - so rapidly skipping tracks leaves multiple overlapping gain ramps racing each other, and the displayed 'now playing' track can end up audibly wrong (fading in a track that was already skipped past) even though the timeout-based swap itself is correctly cancelled.
key_learnings: Correctly found and cancelled the stale setTimeout on rapid track changes, confirming via the test's timer-count assertion that only one timeout is ever pending at a time.
mistakes: Treated the exercise as solved once the timeout leak was fixed, without noticing the gain-ramp (the actual audio fade-in/out driven by a separate requestAnimationFrame loop started inside the same effect) has no cancellation path at all - it was never covered by the cleanup function that was written, so it keeps running after a skip even once the timeout half is fixed correctly.

Final run: 3/5 passing - both tests that simulate rapid double-skips and assert only one gain ramp is active at a time still fail, confirming the overlapping-ramp race is still present after the submitted fix.

When the second failing test was pointed out, misdiagnosed it as a flaky/timing-sensitive test issue rather than re-examining whether the cleanup function actually tore down everything the effect had started.
next_focus: When an effect starts more than one ongoing thing (here: a timeout AND a separate rAF-driven ramp), check that the cleanup function tears down every one of them individually - cancelling one is not evidence the others are handled too.

Before concluding a fix is done, re-read the effect's setup from top to bottom and list every subscription/timer/animation it starts, then confirm each has a matching line in the returned cleanup - rather than stopping once the first obviously-leaking piece is fixed.

Don't default to 'flaky test' as an explanation for a failure before re-checking the fix itself, especially on a test that's deterministically simulating a specific user action (here, two skips in quick succession).

title: Fare Upgrade Engine
flaw: isUpgradeEligible(booking) both answers 'can this booking be upgraded' AND, as a side effect, decrements the shared seatInventory pool and writes an upgradeOfferExpiresAt timestamp onto the booking - so a 'what if' eligibility check from the UI (e.g. hovering an upsell banner, or checking eligibility for display purposes) silently consumes real inventory and starts a real offer-expiry countdown, even if the customer never clicks anything. A query/command-separation violation one level more subtle than a typical 'getter with a side effect', since the side effects are partial/conditional rather than unconditional.
key_learnings: Correctly identified the core problem as the eligibility check doing real work (inventory decrement, timestamp write) rather than only answering a question.
Attempted a split into a pure isUpgradeEligible query and a separate reserveUpgradeOffer command, which is the right overall shape.
mistakes: The split was only applied at the call site used by the upsell banner - a second call site (the booking-confirmation modal) still calls the original combined function directly, so the query/command conflation still exists and is reachable from production code, just no longer from the one spot that was being looked at.

`reserveUpgradeOffer`'s inventory decrement does not check whether the offer was already reserved for this booking before decrementing again, so calling it twice for the same booking (e.g. a double-click, or the two call sites both eventually calling it) double-decrements seatInventory - a new bug introduced by the split that didn't exist in the original combined function, where the condition at least made each decrement path self-limiting in a way this version lost.
Test run against the submitted branch: 4/6 passing - the two failures are the double-decrement case and the still-combined confirmation-modal path, both pre-existing in this submission, not flaky.
review_changes: Traced both call sites (upsell banner and confirmation modal) to show the fix is incomplete - only one was migrated.
Walked through the double-decrement scenario step by step with the submitted reserveUpgradeOffer to show where the missing idempotency check would need to go.

Deferred to the next session for a redo on both: finish migrating the confirmation modal to use the pure query, and add a guard so reserveUpgradeOffer is safe to call more than once for the same booking (either a no-op on repeat, or an explicit error) - same category/difficulty held per the needs_revision rule.
next_focus: After splitting a query from a command, grep/search for every call site of the ORIGINAL combined function - a partial split that leaves even one caller on the old combined path reintroduces the exact bug for that caller.

When a command used to be gated by a condition that happened to also prevent it from double-firing, re-examine whether extracting it as a standalone command lost that protection - 'it was safe before' doesn't mean it's still safe once the shape changes.

title: Course Enrollment Engine
flaw: attemptEnrollment conflates checking enrollment eligibility (prerequisites, schedule conflict, credit hour limit, seat availability) with committing it: a successful check also decrements section.seatsAvailable, pushes onto student.schedule, and increases student.currentCreditHours as a side effect, so there's no way to safely preview eligibility (e.g. for a 'Would I get in?' course-planner tool) without also consuming a seat and enrolling the student - same query/command-separation smell as the prior (needs_revision) exercise, held at the same category and difficulty since that one's fix didn't reach the public API. Domain changed to education to avoid repeating travel/airline.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed that the fix needed to land on the public API: exported `canEnroll(section, student)` as a pure, side-effect-free preview, and had `attemptEnrollment` delegate to it - mutating `seatsAvailable`/`schedule`/`currentCreditHours` only once `canEnroll` returns eligible. This is exactly the gap that sent the prior Fare Upgrade Engine exercise back for revision (its split stayed module-private).
Wired the bonus audit log so it only pushes from `attemptEnrollment`'s commit path, not from `canEnroll`'s preview path - matches the bonus's 'every committed enrollment, not every check' ask.
Preserved the four eligibility rules and their original order (prerequisites, time conflict, credit limit, seat availability) while doing the split, per the restriction.
mistakes: The audit log entry is built as `{...section, id: student.id}`, which spreads the whole `Section` object (including its own `id`, e.g. 'CS201-A') and then immediately overwrites that same-named `id` key with the student's id. Confirmed by running it: the logged entry's `id` ends up as the student's id, and the section's own id is silently discarded - only `courseCode` survives, so two sections of the same course (two time slots of CS201, say) would be indistinguishable in the log. Undercuts the bonus's own stated goal ('how many students enrolled in *this section*').
review_changes: Ran the submitted branch (`courseenrollment`) against the exercise's own test suite and `tsc --noEmit`: 5/5 passing, clean compile.

Probed the exact scenario from the README's breaking point: a section with one seat left, two students both calling `canEnroll` any number of times before either commits. Confirmed `canEnroll` never touches `section.seatsAvailable` no matter who calls it or how many times, and only the real `attemptEnrollment` call consumes the seat - the second student correctly gets 'Section is full.' once the first has committed. This is the exact guarantee the prior exercise was missing.
Ran the submitted branch (`courseenrollment`) against the exercise's own test suite and `tsc --noEmit`: 5/5 passing, clean compile.

Probed the exact scenario from the README's breaking point: a section with one seat left, two students both calling `canEnroll` any number of times before either commits. Confirmed `canEnroll` never touches `section.seatsAvailable` no matter who calls it or how many times, and only the real `attemptEnrollment` call consumes the seat - the second student correctly gets 'Section is full.' once the first has committed. This is the exact guarantee the prior exercise was missing.
Reproduced the audit-log push by hand to confirm the `id` field ends up as the student's id rather than the section's, confirming the courseCode-only identification gap.
next_focus: When building a logged/derived shape from two different entities that happen to share a field name (here, both `Section` and `Student` have an `id`), name the two fields distinctly in the merged shape (`sectionId`/`studentId`) instead of spreading one entity and overwriting a same-named field from the other - spread-then-override order is a silent trap.

title: Lookup Cache Trio
flaw: PolicyCache, ClaimCache, and MemberCache are three structurally identical classes (a Map-backed get/set/has/delete/size cache), differing only in which entity type they hold, with no generic abstraction tying them together - so adding a fourth entity's cache (e.g. CoverageCache) means copy-pasting the same logic a fourth time, and nothing stops a fifth or sixth copy from drifting out of sync with the others. Regenerated under the updated EXERCISE_SPEC.md (category now strictly round-robins every exercise instead of holding while the prior exercise sits unreviewed) to replace the original 10-10-2026 exercise, Showing Slot Booker, which had repeated the exact same query-command-separation smell as exercises 10 and 11, just reskinned - see the spec's revision notes. First appearance of the missing-generics pattern.

title: Live Leaderboard Panel
flaw: LeaderboardPanel computes 'who's leading' inside a useEffect keyed on the scores array reference and stores it in its own state, instead of deriving it directly during render - so when a prospective 'Live Mode' feature updates the scores array in place (mutating entries on the same array object for performance rather than building a new array each tick), the effect's dependency comparison sees no reference change, never re-runs, and the displayed leader goes stale even though the underlying step counts have clearly moved. Confirmed directly: mutating scores in place and rerendering with the same array reference leaves the displayed leader unchanged. Regenerated under the updated EXERCISE_SPEC.md (category now strictly round-robins every exercise) to replace the original 10-11-2026 exercise, Device Rollout Scheduler, which had repeated the exact same query-command-separation smell as exercises 10, 11, and the original 10-10 exercise - see the spec's revision notes. First appearance of the derived-state-duplicated pattern.

title: Batch Release Rules
flaw: canStageForPicking and canApproveShipment independently re-implement the same batch-quality-release rule rather than sharing one source of truth, and the two copies have already drifted: canStageForPicking blocks quarantined batches from any destination except QUARANTINE_HOLD, but canApproveShipment never grew that check (its comment says quarantine holds didn't exist when direct-to-customer shipping launched, so recalled was the only status it ever needed to block), so a quarantined batch can currently be approved for shipment straight to a regular facility - a duplicated-business-rule-gone-stale smell, same shape as exercise 8.
